idiom_name: private _impl module plus __all__ and the underscore convention
implementation_notes: Python has no compile step and no header, so the pattern becomes a module-layout convention: keep the body in an underscore-prefixed module or package (_impl.py, _internals/), re-export only the public names from the package __init__, and declare __all__ so wildcard imports and tooling see the same surface - a single leading underscore is the documented signal that a name is not part of the API, and from module import * honours __all__. Where a real opaque handle is required it lives at the C-extension boundary, where a type defined only inside the extension and passed around as a PyCapsule (part of the Stable ABI) is the exact analogue of the pointer. The classic delegating wrapper class is not worth writing in pure Python: it adds an indirection per call and buys nothing the module system does not already give.
pitfalls: Underscore privacy is a convention enforced only by from x import * and reader discipline: importing the submodule directly, getattr or poking at module attributes reaches the body, so renaming internals breaks someone in practice even though the name is private.
Name mangling (double leading underscore inside a class) only rewrites the attribute to _Class__name to avoid subclass clashes; it is not privacy and does not stop setattr.
A wheel ships the implementation files, so hidden code is still readable and patchable in the installed environment - this protects the import surface and refactoring freedom, not secrets.
